title: What we have handled (1 John 1:1–4)
hook: the word of life that we have seen and touched

segments.voice: Yesterday, makrothymei: a God with a very long fuse. Your line was he is patient.

You can read everything about the ocean, tides, salt, the color of deep water, and watch it in videos for hours. Then one day you stand at the edge and a cold wave runs over your feet, and the water teaches what the books couldn't. Hearing about it, seeing it, touching it: three different kinds of knowing. The first letter of John doesn't open with a greeting or a name. It opens with a witness, an old man, as tradition pictures him, saying: I'm not passing on a rumor. I was there. I touched him.
screen: `READING ABOUT THE OCEAN.` → `A COLD WAVE OVER YOUR FEET.` → `I WAS THERE. I TOUCHED HIM.`

segments.voice: Listen to the sentence move, in the Douay-Rheims: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the word of life." It starts at the very start of everything, from the beginning, an echo of the opening of John's Gospel. Then it comes closer, step by step. Heard: across a room. Seen: now he's in view. Looked upon: a long, steady gaze. And handled: hands on. The Word that was with God from the beginning is something a fisherman could put his hand on. Why insist? Some scholars think the letter was answering people who said Jesus only seemed to have a body, that God would never really take on flesh, get tired, bleed. John won't have it. Later in the letter he says that every spirit which confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is of God. The Greek word for handled is the same one the risen Jesus uses in Luke's Gospel, when the frightened disciples think he's a spirit: handle, and see. And notice why John writes: so that you may have fellowship with us, and our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son. The Greek is koinonia, which comes into Catholic language as communion. And so that our joy may be full. For Catholics this touchable faith runs through the sacraments: water on a forehead, oil on hands, bread placed on a tongue or in a palm. God, in this tradition, keeps coming close enough to touch.
screen: `FROM THE BEGINNING, THEN CLOSER.` · `HEARD, SEEN, LOOKED UPON, HANDLED.` · `NOT A GHOST: COME IN THE FLESH.` · `KOINONIA: FELLOWSHIP, COMMUNION.` · then, large: `OUR HANDS HAVE HANDLED THE WORD OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Hold something near you, a cross, a rosary, a smooth stone, or just your own palm, and feel its weight, its temperature, its edges. Let it stand for a faith that says God came close enough to touch. If you pray, hold it as a prayer without words; if not, stay with the plain fact of touch and notice what your hands know.
Koinonia, fellowship. First John one: the word of life, heard, seen, looked upon and touched, so that we may share this fellowship together. Today's word.
Your line: seen and touched. Heard, seen, looked upon, and handled by human hands. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic sacraments are celebrated with things that can be seen and touched, water, oil, bread, wine and the laying on of hands, and Catholics may keep a rosary, cross or medal close as a physical reminder of their faith.

original.note: Greek: (our hands) have handled (1 John 1:1). from psēlaphaō, to touch, to feel.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poetic way to say the apostles knew Jesus.
what it means: the Word that was from the beginning came close enough to hear, see and touch, and that's the root of the fellowship John offers.
what a scholar hears: psēlaphaō, the verb of the risen Christ in Luke 24:39, 'handle, and see'; some scholars think the letter answers those who denied his real flesh.
recall: the inner sanctuary of a temple

chat.says: Why does John's letter make such a big deal about touching Jesus?
options: He insists Jesus really came in the flesh, not a ghost: heard, seen and handled.
He's saying only those who touched Jesus can really believe in him.
He's describing healings that came from touching Jesus's cloak.
chat.meaning: John stresses heard, seen, looked upon and handled: the word of life came in the flesh, close enough to touch, so readers share in koinonia.

koinonia.meaning: Greek: fellowship; in Catholic language, communion

word of life.meaning: John's name for Christ, heard, seen and touched

sacraments.meaning: Catholic rites like baptism, using water, oil and bread

Douay-Rheims.meaning: the old Catholic English translation of the Bible

sources.quoted: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the word of life

notes: Tradition identifies the writer with John the apostle, an old man at Ephesus; the script says 'as tradition pictures him'. Authorship is discussed by scholars. Confirm framing.
'Some scholars think the letter was answering people who said Jesus only seemed to have a body' (proto-Docetism) is a common scholarly view, not certain. Confirm.
Psēlaphaō in 1 John 1:1 and Luke 24:39: confirm.
Koinonia → communion: confirm phrasing. 1 John 1:3–4 and 4:2 are paraphrased.
